questions.question:
With reference to Harappan seals and trade, consider the following statements:

 
• Harappan seals often carried animal motifs and short inscriptions.
 
• Standardised weights suggest regulated exchange and commercial activity.
 
• Evidence of Harappan contact with Mesopotamia has been suggested by archaeological findings.
 
• Harappan seals conclusively prove that Sanskrit was the language of the Harappans.

Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** Harappan seals often carried **animal motifs** such as unicorn, bull, elephant, rhinoceros and tiger, along with **short inscriptions**. Hence, **Statement 1 is correct**.
 
• **Statement 2:** The presence of **standardized weights** suggests regulated exchange, trade and commercial activity in the Harappan civilisation. Hence, **Statement 2 is correct**.
 
• **Statement 3:** Archaeological findings suggest Harappan contact with **Mesopotamia**. Mesopotamian references to **Meluhha** are often associated with the Harappan region. Hence, **Statement 3 is correct**.
 
• **Statement 4:** Harappan seals do not conclusively prove that **Sanskrit** was the language of the Harappans. The Harappan script remains **undeciphered**. Hence, **Statement 4 is incorrect**.
 
• Therefore, **Statements 1, 2 and 3 only are correct**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Harappan seals were generally made of **steatite**.
 
• They were likely used for **trade, ownership marking and administrative purposes**.
 
• The **unicorn motif** is one of the most common motifs on Harappan seals.
 
• Trade links existed with **Mesopotamia, Oman and Bahrain/Dilmun**.
 
• Important trade items included **beads, metals, shells, cotton textiles and craft goods**.

questions.question:
With reference to Jain philosophy, consider the following categories:

 
• Deva
 
• Manusya
 
• Tiryanca
 
• Yaksha

Which of the above are included among the recognised forms of existence or destinies of living beings in Jain thought?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **1. Deva:** In Jain thought, **Deva** refers to celestial/heavenly beings and is one of the recognised destinies of living beings. Hence, **1 is correct**.
 
• **2. Manusya:****Manusya** refers to human existence. It is considered highly important in Jainism because liberation is possible through right conduct in human birth. Hence, **2 is correct**.
 
• **3. Tiryanca:****Tiryanca** includes animals, plants and other non-human worldly beings. It is one of the recognised forms of existence. Hence, **3 is correct**.
 
• **4. Yaksha:****Yakshas** are attendant or semi-divine beings associated with Jain tradition, but they are not counted as a separate main destiny/gati of living beings. Hence, **4 is incorrect**.
 
• Therefore, **1, 2 and 3 only are correct**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Jainism recognises four major **gatis** or destinies: **Deva, Manusya, Tiryanca and Naraki**.
 
• The soul takes birth in different gatis according to its **karma**.
 
• Human birth is considered especially valuable because it offers the possibility of **moksha**.
 
• **Yaksha-Yakshini** figures are often associated with Tirthankaras as attendant deities.

questions.question: Which ruler is associated with the introduction of gold coinage on a large scale in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vima Kadphises**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vima Kadphises**, also known as **Kadphises II**, was a powerful **Kushan** emperor who reigned approximately from **95 CE to 127 CE** and is historically credited with the first large-scale introduction of **gold coinage** in India.
 
• The **gold dinars** issued during his reign were minted to facilitate expanding trade with the **Roman Empire**, aligning with the **Roman weight standard** of approximately **8 grams** to ensure economic parity in international commerce.
 
• His coinage featured a distinct transition from the purely **Greek** styles of his predecessors to a more **Indianized** iconographic representation, often depicting the ruler on the **obverse** and the Hindu deity **Lord Shiva** with a trident on the **reverse**.
 
• The inscriptions on these coins were typically **bilingual**, utilizing **Greek script** on one side and **Kharosthi script** on the other, reflecting the **multicultural** governance of the **Kushan Empire** across **North India** and **Central Asia**.
 
• Vima Kadphises assumed grandiose titles such as **Maharaja**, **Rajadhiraja** (King of Kings), and **Sarvaloka Ishvara** (Lord of the whole world), which were prominently stamped on his gold issues to assert **sovereignty**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Comparative Historical Context**:
 
 
• **Chandragupta Maurya** and **Ashoka**: Rulers of the **Mauryan Empire** (4th–3rd century BCE) who primarily utilized **silver punch-marked coins** known as **Pana** or **Karshapana**, rather than standardized gold currency.
 
• **Harsha**: A 7th-century ruler of the **Pushyabhuti dynasty** who issued **gold** and **silver** coins, but his reign occurred centuries after the **initial introduction** of gold currency by the Kushans.
 
• **Kanishka I**: The successor to Vima Kadphises who further popularized **gold coins** and utilized them to spread **Buddhist** imagery and **Iranian** deities across the **Silk Road**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Significance**:
 
 
• The introduction of **high-purity gold** allowed the Kushans to dominate the **Silk Route** trade, acting as intermediaries between the **Han Dynasty** of China and the **Roman Mediterranean**.

questions.question:
Which of the following pairs of Mahajanapada and its capital is/are correctly matched?

 
• Magadha : Rajagriha
 
• Kosala : Shravasti
 
• Vatsa : Kaushambi
 
• Avanti : Taxila

Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pair 1:****Magadha** had its early capital at **Rajagriha/Rajgir**. Later, the capital shifted to **Pataliputra**. Hence, **Pair 1 is correctly matched**.
 
• **Pair 2:****Kosala** had **Shravasti** as an important capital. Hence, **Pair 2 is correctly matched**.
 
• **Pair 3:****Vatsa** had its capital at **Kaushambi**. Hence, **Pair 3 is correctly matched**.
 
• **Pair 4:****Avanti** was associated with **Ujjayini** and **Mahishmati**, not Taxila. **Taxila** was associated with **Gandhara**. Hence, **Pair 4 is incorrectly matched**.
 
• Therefore, **Pairs 1, 2 and 3 only are correctly matched**.
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/5fbaac767ae5df75652dd4ebcc3ffbb3b6891544b53dd7223f10cb13e6b6739b.png] 
 
• 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Mahajanapadas** were major territorial states around the **6th century BCE**.
 
• **Magadha** became powerful due to fertile land, iron resources, elephants and strategic location.
 
• **Rajagriha** was associated with early Magadhan rulers like **Bimbisara and Ajatashatru**.
 
• **Taxila** was an important centre of learning and trade in **Gandhara**, not Avanti.

questions.question: What does an empty throne or empty seat often represent in early Buddhist art?

options.text: The presence or enlightenment of the Buddha without depicting him in human form
The decline of the Buddhist Sangha.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Option 1:** The empty throne or empty seat in early Buddhist art does not represent the renunciation of **Mahavira**. Mahavira is associated with Jainism, not Buddhist symbolism. Hence, **Option 1 is incorrect**.
 
• **Option 2:** In early Buddhist art, the Buddha was often represented through **symbols** rather than in human form. An **empty throne/empty seat** symbolised the **presence of the Buddha** or his **enlightenment**. Hence, **Option 2 is correct**.
 
• **Option 3:** The empty throne does not represent the coronation of **Ashoka**. Hence, **Option 3 is incorrect**.
 
• **Option 4:** It does not symbolise the decline of the Buddhist Sangha. Hence, **Option 4 is incorrect**.
 
• Therefore, **an empty throne or empty seat represents the presence or enlightenment of the Buddha without depicting him in human form**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Early Buddhist art followed an **aniconic tradition**, where Buddha was represented through symbols.
 
• Common symbols include **empty throne, Bodhi tree, footprints, wheel and stupa**.
 
• The **Bodhi tree** represents enlightenment.
 
• The **wheel/Dharmachakra** represents the first sermon and teaching of Dharma.
 
• The **footprints** symbolise the Buddha’s presence and spiritual path.

questions.question: The celebrated Sanskrit poet Kalidasa is believed to have flourished in the court of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chandragupta II**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kalidasa** is widely regarded as the most prominent **Sanskrit** poet and dramatist of ancient India, whose literary works represent the pinnacle of classical Indian aesthetics.
 
• He is historically associated with the court of the **Gupta monarch Chandragupta II**, who assumed the prestigious title of **Vikramaditya** and ruled from approximately **380 CE to 415 CE**.
 
• Traditional accounts identify Kalidasa as the foremost of the **Navaratnas** (Nine Jewels), a group of extraordinary scholars and artists who graced the royal court at **Ujjain**.
 
• His literary mastery is immortalized in the play **Abhijnanashakuntalam**, which was among the first Indian literary works to be translated into European languages, earning global recognition for Indian drama.
 
• The reign of **Chandragupta II** is celebrated as a significant part of the **Golden Age of India**, a period marked by unprecedented peace, prosperity, and advancements in literature, science, and the arts.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Samudragupta**:
 
 
• Known as the **Napoleon of India**, he was a great conqueror and a patron of arts, often depicted on his coins playing the **Veena**.
 
• His achievements are inscribed on the **Prayag Prashasti** (Allahabad Pillar) composed by his court poet **Harisena**.
 
 
 
• **Skandagupta**:
 
 
• He was the last major ruler of the **Gupta Dynasty**, famous for defending the empire against the invasions of the **Hunas**.
 
• He is remembered for his administrative skills and for restoring the **Sudarshana Lake** in Junagadh.
 
 
 
• **Ashoka**:
 
 
• The third ruler of the **Mauryan Empire** (c. 268−232 BCE), known for his conversion to **Buddhism** after the **Kalinga War** and his propagation of **Dhamma**.
 
 
 
• **Kalidasa's Notable Works**:
 
 
• His major contributions include the mahakavyas **Raghuvamsa** and **Kumarasambhava**, and lyrical poems like **Meghaduta** and **Ritusamhara**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Consider the following pairs:

 
 

 
 
**Dynasty**

 
 
 
**Cultural/Political Association**

 
 
 

 
 
I. Palas

 
 
 
Patronage to Mahayana Buddhist institutions

 
 
 

 
 
II. Pratiharas

 
 
 
Maritime expansion into Southeast Asia

 
 
 

 
 
III. Rashtrakutas

 
 
 
Rock-cut architectural patronage in the Deccan

 
 
 

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pair I:** The **Pala dynasty**, which ruled parts of eastern India including Bengal and Bihar, is well known for its patronage to **Mahayana Buddhism**. The Palas supported major Buddhist centres such as **Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri**. Hence, **Pair I is correctly matched**.
 
• **Pair II:** The **Pratiharas** were primarily a north Indian power associated with resistance against Arab expansion and participation in the **Tripartite Conflict**. They were not known for major maritime expansion into Southeast Asia. Such maritime activities are more closely associated with dynasties like the **Cholas**. Hence, **Pair II is incorrectly matched**.
 
• **Pair III:** The **Rashtrakutas** are associated with significant contributions to **rock-cut architecture** in the Deccan region. The famous **Kailasa Temple at Ellora** was constructed during Rashtrakuta rule and represents an important achievement in Indian rock-cut architecture. Hence, **Pair III is correctly matched**.
 
• Therefore, **only two pairs are correctly matched**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Pala dynasty flourished approximately between the **8th and 12th centuries CE**.
 
• The **Kailasa Temple at Ellora** is attributed largely to the Rashtrakuta ruler **Krishna I**.
 
• The Gurjara-Pratiharas played an important role in controlling parts of northern and western India during the early medieval period.
 
• The Palas maintained cultural and religious links with regions such as **Tibet and Southeast Asia** through Buddhist networks.
 
• The Rashtrakutas patronized literature in languages such as **Sanskrit and Kannada**.

questions.question: In Buddhist rock-cut architecture, which type of structure served as the dwelling place for Buddhist monks?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Viharas**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• In the context of **Buddhist architecture**, a **Vihara** refers to a monastery or a residential complex for **Buddhist monks** (**Bhikkhus**) and nuns.

• The concept originated from the need for a permanent shelter during the rainy season, a period known as **Vassa**, when wandering monks were required to stay in one place to avoid trampling on new plant growth and insects.

• Structurally, a rock-cut **Vihara** typically consists of a central square or rectangular hall surrounded by several small, narrow **cells** that served as individual living quarters for the monks.

• Most of these residential units were carved into hillsides and are found in proximity to **Chaityas**, which served as the prayer or congregational halls.

• Major archaeological sites showcasing these structures include the **Ajanta Caves**, **Ellora Caves**, **Kanheri Caves**, and **Karle Caves** in **Maharashtra**, which highlight the evolution from simple stone cells to decorated multi-storeyed apartments.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Chaitya-Grihas**

• These are the prayer halls associated with **Buddhism**, characterized by a vaulted roof and a **Stupa** placed at the end of the apse for circumambulation.

• **Mandapas**

• These are pillared outdoor halls or porches used for public rituals and ceremonies in **Hindu temple architecture**, acting as a transition space between the entrance and the **Garbhagriha**.

• **Gopurams**

• These are monumental entrance towers, often ornately decorated with sculptures, typical of the **Dravidian style** of architecture in South Indian temples.

• **Prakaras**

• These represent the massive enclosure walls that surround the main deity and the inner temple complex in **South Indian architecture**, creating a sacred boundary.

</ul

questions.question: Which of the following metals was unaware to the Harappan Civilization people?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Harappan Civilization**, also known as the **Indus Valley Civilization**, is archaeologically classified as a **Bronze Age** culture that flourished approximately between **3300 BCE and 1300 BCE**.
 
• Extensive archaeological excavations across major sites like **Mohenjo-daro**, **Harappa**, and **Lothal** have unearthed a variety of metallic artifacts, but there is a complete absence of **Iron** objects in the **Harappan** strata.
 
• The **Iron Age** in India began significantly later, during the **Vedic Period**, with the earliest evidence of **Iron** smelting found at sites like **Atranjikhera** dating to around **1000 BCE**.
 
• Harappan craftsmen were experts in the **lost-wax technique** (Cire Perdue) for casting **Bronze**, but the high melting point required for **Iron** extraction was a technological milestone they had not yet achieved.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Copper**:
 
 
• It was the primary metal used by the Harappans, often sourced from the **Khetri mines** in **Rajasthan**.
 
• It was used to manufacture **chisels**, **knives**, **fish-hooks**, and **mirrors**.
 
 
 
• **Gold**:
 
 
• Commonly used for making **jewelry** such as beads, pendants, and armlets.
 
• Likely sourced from the **Kolar mines** in **Karnataka** or through river panning in the **Himalayan** region.
 
 
 
• **Silver**:
 
 
• The **Harappans** provided the earliest evidence of **Silver** usage in India.
 
• It was primarily used to create **vessels**, **seals**, and large luxury ornaments, often imported from **Afghanistan** or **Iran**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which one of the following best explains the significance of standardized weights and measures in the Harappan civilisation?

options.text: They indicate the absence of trade and exchange.
They suggest regulated exchange, craft production and commercial transactions.
They prove that Harappans used coins made of silver and gold.
They show that agriculture was unknown to the Harappans.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Option 1:** Standardized weights and measures do not indicate absence of trade. Rather, they strongly suggest organised trade and exchange. Hence, **Option 1 is incorrect**.
 
• **Option 2:** The use of **standardized weights and measures** in the Harappan civilisation suggests regulated exchange, craft production and commercial transactions. It indicates that the Harappans had a well-organised economic system. Hence, **Option 2 is correct**.
 
• **Option 3:** Standardized weights do not prove the use of coins made of silver and gold. Coinage was not a feature of the Harappan civilisation. Hence, **Option 3 is incorrect**.
 
• **Option 4:** Standardized weights and measures do not show that agriculture was unknown. The Harappans practised agriculture along with trade, craft production and animal domestication. Hence, **Option 4 is incorrect**.
 
• Therefore, standardized weights and measures indicate **regulated exchange, craft production and commercial transactions**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Harappan weights were often made of **chert** and followed a binary or decimal system.
 
• Standardized weights helped in maintaining uniformity in trade and exchange across distant settlements.
 
• Seals, weights and measures together suggest organised commercial activity.
 
• Craft production included **bead-making, pottery, metallurgy, shell-working and seal-making**.
 
• The presence of standardized weights across different Harappan sites reflects a high degree of cultural and economic integration.
